title: Abraham ibn Ezra
hook: traveler, poet, grammarian and sharp-eyed commentator

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bahya's Duties of the Heart. Your line was the greater war is inside. Today, a man who couldn't stay put.

If I sold candles, the sun would never set. That's the gist of a short Hebrew poem, a joke a poet made about his own luck. If he dealt in burial shrouds, he goes on, nobody would die as long as he lived. Whatever he tried, the world arranged itself so that he couldn't make a living. The man who wrote that was not a failure. He was a sharp-eyed reader of the Bible, a grammarian, an astronomer, a poet, and a wanderer who carried his books from city to city. Today, Abraham ibn Ezra.
screen: `CANDLES, AND THE SUN NEVER SETS.` → `A POET LAUGHS AT HIS LUCK.` → `A WANDERER WITH BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ezra grew up in Muslim Spain, in the world of the poets we've met this week. Then he left, and kept moving: Italy, France and, by his own writings, as far as England. Wherever he stayed, he wrote. Spanish Jewish learning had grown up in Arabic, and Arabic was not the language of the Jews of Christian Europe. So ibn Ezra did something simple and huge: he wrote it out in Hebrew. Grammar books, astronomy, and above all commentaries on the Bible. As a commentator he wanted the plain meaning of the words, what Hebrew calls peshat. He paid close attention to grammar: how a verb is built, why a word is spelled the way it is. He could be blunt with interpretations he thought ignored the words on the page. And he had a sharp eye for the odd detail. When Abram first arrives in the land, Genesis says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And the Canaanite was then in the land." Then? Ibn Ezra noticed that little word. He wrote that there is a secret here, and that the one who understands it should keep silent. He doesn't say what the secret is. Readers have argued ever since: some read it as a hint about who wrote that line and when; others read it differently. That's very ibn Ezra: sharp, brief, and willing to leave a question hanging. A traveler learns to notice what locals stop seeing. Maybe that's why he saw so much in a word like then. He left behind commentaries that Jews still print beside the Torah.
screen: `A WANDERER: ITALY, FRANCE, ENGLAND.` · `SPANISH LEARNING CARRIED INTO HEBREW.` · `PESHAT: THE PLAIN MEANING.` · then, large: `AND THE CANAANITE WAS THEN IN THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Say the verse once, slowly: and the Canaanite was then in the land. Now read it the way ibn Ezra did: which word stops you, and what question would you write in the margin? You don't need an answer; if you pray, you can ask in your own words to read with open eyes.
Ibn Ezra. A wandering poet, grammarian and Bible commentator from Spain who looked for the plain meaning, peshat, in every verse. Today's word.
Your line: the traveler. Fresh eyes catch the small word everyone else skips. Day nine hundred twenty-six, done.

howItsDone: Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary is printed alongside the Torah in editions of the Mikraot Gedolot, the rabbinic Bible, and students read him for his attention to grammar and plain meaning.
